ru-d-chaikovsky.s: The composer Pyotr Tchaikovsky wrote the music for the ballet “The Nutcracker”. For the dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy he needed a very special sound, like little drops of glass. He brought a new instrument from Paris, the celesta. It looks like a small piano with little bells inside. People say he wanted the sound to be a surprise for the audience, so he kept it secret until the first night. In the town of Klin, near Moscow, there is a house where he wrote music. Now it is a museum.

ru-d-gagarin.s: On the 12th of April 1961, a rocket lifted off from the Baikonur space centre. Yuri Gagarin was sitting in the spaceship Vostok. Before the start he cheerfully shouted, “Poyekhali!”, which means “Let’s go!” He flew once around the whole Earth and came back. The whole flight took 108 minutes, less than two hours. From space Gagarin saw that our planet is blue, and he told the people on Earth. Today that day is called Cosmonautics Day.

ru-suzdal.s: Suzdal is a small, very old town in the Golden Ring. That is the name of a trip through ancient Russian towns that makes a ring on the map. In Suzdal there is an open-air museum. Old wooden village houses and windmills were brought there from the villages. You can go inside a house and see a big Russian stove. And in summer Suzdal has a funny festival: Cucumber Day!

ru-khokhloma.s: Khokhloma is golden painting on wooden dishes: spoons, bowls and cups. Red berries, black leaves and curls seem to glow on the golden background. But there is no real gold there! The craftsmen rub the dishes with silvery powder, paint the pattern, cover it with varnish and put it in a hot oven. The heat turns the varnish yellow, and the silvery dishes become golden.
a: From the varnish and the heat of the oven

ru-gzhel.s: Gzhel is white and blue pottery and little figures. They are made in a region with the same name, not far from Moscow. The craftsman paints flowers, birds and curls on white dishes with a brush. It is amazing, but at first the paint is dark, almost black. Then the dishes are baked in a very hot oven, and the pattern turns bright blue, like the spring sky.

ru-dymka.s: The Dymkovo toy comes from the town of Kirov. The craftswomen shape ladies in big, puffy skirts, turkeys, horses and little goats from clay. Then the toy is whitened with chalk mixed with milk, and it becomes white, white, white. On top they paint bright circles, stripes and squares: red, yellow and blue. And long ago many of these toys were whistles.

ru-tula.s: The city of Tula is famous for samovars and gingerbread. A samovar is a big shiny kettle with a pipe inside. Long ago, people put hot embers or pine cones into the pipe, and the water boiled quickly. And a Tula gingerbread is flat, with a jam filling. A pattern is pressed on top with a wooden board, like a stamp.

ru-kazan.s: Kazan stands on the bank of the Volga. It has a white Kremlin, and in it there is the Syuyumbike Tower. It leans a little, as if it were tired of standing. In Kazan people speak two languages: Russian and Tatar. The most famous Tatar treat is chak-chak. These are little pieces of dough that are fried, covered with honey and piled up in a heap.

ru-sochi.s: Sochi is a warm city on the shore of the Black Sea. In summer everybody swims and sunbathes there. Palm trees grow in its streets, and snow rarely falls in the city itself. But very close by, in the mountains of Krasnaya Polyana, there is lots of snow in winter. In spring you can walk under the palm trees in the morning and go sledging in the afternoon! In 2014 the Winter Olympic Games were held in Sochi.

ru-amber.s: The Kaliningrad region is the most western land of Russia. Here, by the Baltic Sea, more amber is dug than anywhere else in the world. Amber is the resin of ancient trees that hardened and became a warm, honey-yellow little stone. Sometimes you can see a fly or an ant inside, stuck in the resin a very, very long time ago. And after a storm people walk along the beach and find pieces of amber right in the sand.
a: From the resin of ancient trees

ru-polar-bears.s: Far away in the north, in the cold ocean, lies Wrangel Island. It is called the maternity ward of polar bears. In autumn the mother bears dig dens in the snow, and in winter tiny blind cubs are born there. In spring the mother leads her little ones out. And do you know, a polar bear has black skin! Its hairs are clear and only look white.

ru-altai.s: Altai is a land of high mountains, fast rivers and cedar forests. Among the mountains lies the long, deep Lake Teletskoye. The people of Altai call it Altyn-Kol, which means Golden Lake. About seventy rivers flow into it, but only one flows out: the River Biya. Then the Biya meets the River Katun, and together they become the great River Ob. The water in the lake is clear and cold, even in summer.

ru-kungur.s: Near the town of Kungur in the Urals there is an Ice Cave. In its first halls it is freezing even in summer, and the walls and ceiling are covered with ice and crystals that look like big snowflakes. The halls of the cave are called grottoes, and there are very many of them. Inside, dozens of underground lakes also hide, with clear, clear water. Visitors are led through the cave with little lamps and coloured lights.

ru-a-tsar-pushka.s: In the Moscow Kremlin there stands a giant cannon. Its name is the Tsar Cannon. Its barrel is longer than a car, more than five metres, and it weighs about thirty-nine tons. A craftsman called Andrey Chokhov cast it in 1586. On the barrel there are beautiful patterns and even a rider on a horse. Next to it lie huge round cannonballs, but they are only there for show. Today the Tsar Cannon is simply an old wonder of skill, and people come from all over the world to see it.

ru-a-tsar-kolokol.s: In the Kremlin there stands a bell that is thought to be the biggest in the world. It is as tall as a house with two floors, more than six metres, and it weighs more than two hundred tons. But the Tsar Bell has never rung, not once. During a big fire a crack appeared in it, and a piece heavier than ten tons broke off. The bell lay in a pit for a long time, and then it was lifted out and put on a stone stand. Now the piece stands beside it, and everyone can look inside the bell.
a: It flew away in a balloon

ru-a-kreml-bashni.s: The Kremlin is surrounded by a red brick wall more than two kilometres long. It has twenty towers, and almost all of them are different: some have tall pointed roofs, others have roofs like hats. Every tower has its own name: Spasskaya, Borovitskaya, Tsarskaya. And on top of the wall there are battlements shaped like a swallow’s tail, more than a thousand of them. If you stand on Red Square and look up, it seems that the towers reach for the clouds.

ru-a-tretyakovka.s: Long ago in Moscow there lived a merchant called Pavel Tretyakov. He loved Russian paintings very much and bought pictures by artists so that everyone could look at them. He collected so many that in 1892 he gave his collection to Moscow. That is how the Tretyakov Gallery began. Its fairy-tale front in Russian style was drawn by the artist Viktor Vasnetsov. Inside hang famous paintings: “Alyonushka”, “Three Heroes” and “Morning in a Pine Forest” with its bear cubs.

ru-a-novgorod-beresta.s: In Veliky Novgorod, about a thousand years ago, people wrote letters on birch bark. They scratched the letters with a sharp stick. Archaeologists found such letters in the ground, and they have survived! Among them are the pages of a boy called Onfim. He was about six or seven years old, and he was learning to write and practising his letters. And between the letters he drew little people and funny animals. These drawings stayed in the ground for almost eight hundred years.

ru-a-yaroslavl-medved.s: There is a bear on the coat of arms of Yaroslavl. It stands on its back legs and holds an axe. An old legend says that Prince Yaroslav the Wise founded the city on the bank of the Volga, in the place where a bear lived, and he beat the bear. That is why the bear became the sign of the city. Today in Yaroslavl the bear is everywhere: on souvenirs, in the streets and on the coat of arms. If you come, look for it on the houses and in the shop windows.

ru-a-vladimir-zolotye-vorota.s: In Vladimir stands the Golden Gate. Prince Andrey Bogolyubsky built it more than eight hundred and fifty years ago from white stone. It was the entrance gate to the city, and above the passage they put a small church. People say the gate leaves were covered with golden-coloured copper, and that is why the gate was called golden. Over so many centuries the gate has lived through rain, frost and rebuilding, but it still stands and lets people and cars pass through.

ru-a-kaliningrad-ostrov-kanta.s: In Kaliningrad, in the middle of the River Pregolya, lies an island, and on it a tall brick cathedral. The city used to be called Königsberg. The scholar Immanuel Kant lived here. They say he hardly ever travelled far from his home town, and still he thought up many things about the whole world. His grave is next to the cathedral. The island is called Kant Island, and a park grows there. And in the cathedral people listen to the sounds of a big organ.

ru-a-nizhny-chkalovskaya.s: In Nizhny Novgorod there is a long staircase that goes down to the Volga. It is called the Chkalov Stairs, after the pilot Valery Chkalov. It is fun to look at from above: it zigzags and looks like the number eight. It has about five hundred and sixty steps, though people count them in different ways. Children like to try to count them all, and then they get different numbers. At the top you can stop and look at the river.

ru-a-ekaterinburg-granitsa.s: Yekaterinburg stands in the Urals, and the Ural Mountains are the border between Europe and Asia. Outside the city there is a big monument, the obelisk “Europe – Asia”. The line of the border runs through the middle. If you stand on it with one foot on one side and the other foot on the other, you are standing in two parts of the world at once. Tourists love to have their photo taken like this: one foot in Europe and the other in Asia.
a: Stand with one foot in Europe and the other in Asia

ru-a-vladivostok-most.s: In Vladivostok there is an island called Russky. To get to it, they built the huge Russky Bridge. It hangs from thick steel cables, and between its tall towers the distance is more than a kilometre: one thousand one hundred and four metres. It is the longest span of any bridge of this kind in the world. The bridge was built in 2012. Ships sail below, cars drive on top, and from the island you can see the sea.

ru-a-salekhard-polyarny-krug.s: Salekhard is a northern city that stands almost exactly on the line of the Arctic Circle. Scientists drew this line on the map, and in the city a memorial sign was put up. The word “Salekhard” comes from the Nenets, the reindeer herders of the tundra. It means “town on a cape”. In summer the nights here are very bright, and in winter there are long dark days. People in Salekhard wear warm fur hats, and in the streets you can meet reindeer.

ru-a-yakutsk-svai.s: In Yakutsk it is so cold in winter that the ground freezes hundreds of metres deep and never thaws. This is called permafrost. If you put an ordinary warm house straight onto it, the ice under it would start to melt and the house would tilt. So in Yakutsk houses are put on long piles driven deep into the frozen ground. Air is left under the house, the wind blows through it and keeps the ground cold. The house stands firm.
a: So that the warmth does not melt the frozen ground
So that the sea does not wash them away
To live closer to the birds

ru-a-arkhangelsk-kozuli.s: In Arkhangelsk, in the North, people bake special gingerbread. It is called kozuli. These are not ordinary gingerbreads but whole pictures: the baker draws reindeer, cows, birds, little fir trees and patterns on them with coloured icing. The Pomors, the people of the shores of the White Sea, used to give kozuli to children on holidays. It seems a pity to eat such a kozulya straight away: you can admire it. But then you still want to try it, because it is sweet.

ru-a-solovki-labirinty.s: On the Solovetsky Islands in the White Sea there are amazing stone labyrinths. They are spirals laid out from stones right on the ground. They are several thousand years old. Why people made them, scientists still argue. Maybe it was a game, or maybe an ancient sign. If you walk along the spiral to the middle and back, you can make a wish. Nearby, in summer, it hardly gets dark.

ru-a-vyborg-biblioteka.s: In Vyborg there is a library built by the famous Finnish architect Alvar Aalto. It was opened back in 1935. Inside there is a lecture hall with a ceiling that goes in waves. And in the reading room there are round little windows in the ceiling, and the light pours through them. The room is built in steps, so the readers sit at different heights. Here everyone finds a comfortable place with a book. This library is famous among architects all over the world.

ru-a-kalyazin-kolokolnya.s: In the town of Kalyazin on the Volga there is a bell tower about seventy-five metres tall, and water all around it. It used to be part of a big cathedral. When a dam was built on the river and a sea appeared, part of the town went under the water. The bottom floor of the bell tower also ended up in the water, but the rest stayed. Now it stands alone on a little island. Ships sail past it, and from far away it looks as if the bell tower is growing straight out of the water.
a: It stands in the middle of the water
It was taken to another planet

ru-a-myshkin-muzei-mishi.s: On the Volga there is a little town with a very fitting name: Myshkin. It has a real Mouse Museum. They say it is the only museum in the world that is only about mice. It holds mice made of wood, clay, glass and cloth, mouse pictures and stories. People bring and send the toys from different countries. That is why Myshkin is called the mouse capital. If you go there, you can have your photo taken with a big mouse.

ru-b-lenskie-stolby.s: Above the River Lena in Yakutia stand stone walls that look like the towers of a fairy-tale castle. Some of them are taller than a hundred-metre building! These rocks are very old: about five hundred million years. And in their cracks scientists find fossil sea animals that lived when there was a warm sea here. Now the place around is cold, and boats sail along the river, while tourists look at the rocks from below and turn their heads this way and that.

ru-b-kurshskaya-kosa.s: The Curonian Spit is a thin strip of sand and pine trees between the sea and a lagoon. It stretches for almost a hundred kilometres. In one place there grows a “dancing forest”: the pine trunks are bent, twisted and curled into rings, as if the trees had started to dance. Why they grew like this, scientists still argue. And nearby rise tall sand dunes, and from Efa Dune you can see both the sea and the lagoon at once.

ru-b-onezhskoe-ozero.s: Lake Onega in Karelia is so big that you cannot see the other shore, just like at the sea. It is the second largest lake in Europe. And it has more than one and a half thousand islands: some huge, some very tiny, where only three fir trees fit. Near the lake people dig a black shiny stone called shungite. It is made into pretty balls that are nice to hold in your hands.
a: More than one and a half thousand

ru-b-klyuchevskaya-sopka.s: In Kamchatka stands the highest active volcano in Eurasia, Klyuchevskaya Sopka. Its top rises higher than four and a half kilometres, and almost always it wears a cap of snow and clouds. From time to time the volcano wakes up: a light puff of smoke rises above it, and sometimes a dark cloud of ash. Other volcanoes stand nearby, and together they look like a family of giants in white hats.

ru-b-ostrov-vrangelya-mamonty.s: On Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean, mammoths lived longer than anywhere else on Earth. When people in Egypt were already building pyramids, small woolly mammoths were still roaming there. They were smaller than their cousins on the mainland. Now musk oxen, reindeer and polar bears live on the island, and thousands of birds nest on the cliffs. The island is a nature reserve, and people may only visit as guests.

ru-b-atomny-ledokol.s: In the Arctic there sails a nuclear icebreaker, a giant ship that makes its own way through the ice. It drives its nose up onto the ice and breaks it with its own weight, and the ice can be more than two metres thick. The icebreaker’s hull is especially strong. Its fuel lasts a long time, and it goes all the way to the North Pole. Passengers stand on the deck and look at the white desert, where there is only sky and ice, and sometimes a polar bear runs by.
a: It drives its nose up onto it and presses with its weight

ru-b-kedrovka.s: In the Siberian taiga lives a bird called the nutcracker. In autumn it gathers cedar nuts and hides them under moss and in the ground, and in a special pouch under its tongue it carries dozens of nuts at once. It has to hide a lot of stores: in winter the nutcracker finds them even under the snow. But some of the hiding places it forgets. New cedar trees grow from the forgotten nuts. So the bird plants a forest by itself, though it does not think about that at all.

ru-b-sobol.s: The sable is a small, nimble animal with soft, warm fur. It lives in the taiga, runs fast over the snow and climbs trees. It likes berries and cedar nuts, and it catches mice. It is cold in Siberia, so even the sable’s paws have thick fur. On the coat of arms of the city of Irkutsk there is a fairy-tale animal called the babr, and it holds a sable in its teeth. In this way the city showed what its land is famous for.

ru-b-amurskiy-goral.s: In the Far East, on the cliffs right by the sea, lives the Amur goral. It looks like a small mountain goat with short horns. Its hooves grip well, so the goral walks on steep cliffs as calmly as we walk on a path. It is hard to see: its grey-brown fur blends in with the rocks, and the animal stands still, like a rock. There are few of these animals, and they are protected.

ru-b-dalnevostochny-leopard.s: In the forests of Primorye lives the rarest big cat in the world, the Far Eastern leopard. Only a little more than a hundred are left, and people very much want to save them. In winter the leopard’s fur is thick and pale, with dark ring-shaped spots scattered over it. Every animal has its own pattern, like fingerprints. Scientists put cameras in the forest and recognise each leopard by its pattern.
a: By the colour of its eyes

ru-b-zubr.s: The European bison is the heaviest land animal in Europe: it weighs almost a ton. Once people almost lost the bison completely, and they were left only in zoos. Then the animals were bred and set free again in the forest, including in the Caucasus and in the Prioksko-Terrasny Reserve near Moscow. Now bison roam through the thickets again, chewing grass and bark, and the bison calves have curly, dark red fur.

ru-b-saygak.s: On the steppes of Kalmykia graze saigas, antelopes with a huge soft nose that looks like a short trunk. The nose is not just for show: in summer it filters the dust that the wind blows up, and in winter it warms the cold air before it goes inside. Saigas run very fast, and there are often many in a herd. People say their ancestors lived even beside the mammoths.
a: To filter dust and warm the air
To drink water from the river

ru-b-golomyanka.s: Deep down in Lake Baikal lives a strange little fish called the golomyanka. It is almost see-through: you can see its tiny bones through its body. The fish is very fatty, and its fat does not freeze in the cold water. The golomyanka does not lay eggs. It gives birth to live baby fish, like a cat has kittens. If you pull it out onto the shore, it melts in the sun like a bit of butter, so not many people get to see it.

ru-b-goryachie-istochniki.s: In Kamchatka, hot springs bubble up out of the ground. There are volcanoes inside the earth, and they heat the water. People build pools by the springs and swim even in winter. Snow lies all around and the frost bites, but the water is warm like a bath. Steam rises over the water, and the bathers’ hats get covered in frost. You can sit there and look at the white hills until your cheeks turn pink.

ru-b-ladozhskaya-nerpa.s: Lake Ladoga is the biggest lake in Europe. It is near St Petersburg and Karelia, and its waves can be as big as in a real sea. But the water is fresh, and seals live in it! Seals are usually found in seas, but in Ladoga they have lived since long, long ago. In winter the seals make holes in the ice and peep out to breathe. The pups are born in snowy dens on the ice.

ru-b-chernoe-more-delfiny.s: Three kinds of dolphin swim in the Black Sea: bottlenose, common and Azov dolphins. The bottlenose is the biggest and the smiliest. The common dolphin looks like it, but it has light patches on its sides. The Azov dolphin is quite small. Dolphins call to each other with whistles and clicks. They sleep in turns: one half of the brain rests while the other half watches so they don’t drown.
a: One half of the brain at a time

ru-b-step-kovyl.s: In the southern steppes of Russia, feather grass grows in spring. Its long silvery plumes bend in the wind, and waves run across the steppe as if it were not grass but the sea. Every feather-grass seed has a sharp little tail, called an awn. When the air is damp, it curls up like a spring and screws the seed into the ground. So the grass plants itself. It doesn’t need a gardener.
a: It curls up and screws the seed into the ground
It rings like a little bell

ru-b-myskusny-byk.s: In the north of Taymyr, where winter is cold and white, lives the musk ox. It looks like a shaggy felt boot with horns. Its long hair hangs almost to the ground, and underneath grows soft, very warm wool, so the frost does not scare the musk ox. Many years ago these animals were brought to Taymyr from another land, and they settled in. Now herds wander across the tundra, looking for grass under the snow.
a: It lives in a warm den

ru-c-shchi-pech.s: Long ago, people did not cook shchi on a cooker but in a Russian stove. The housewife took the pot with an ukhvat, a kind of iron fork with a long handle, and slid it into the warm belly of the stove. The shchi simmered for hours, and tasted special and soft. There is even a saying about it: “Shchi and porridge are our food.” Shchi was made from cabbage. The whole family had wooden spoons, and one shared bowl stood in the middle of the table.

ru-c-yaytsa-luk.s: Before Easter in old Russia, people dyed eggs. The simplest dye was in every kitchen: onion skins. You boil the eggs in water with the skins, and the shells turn reddish-brown, like an autumn leaf. And for the holiday they also bake a tall sweet bread called kulich. It is baked in a narrow tin, so it rises like a chef’s hat. On top it is covered with white sweet icing.

ru-c-sabantuy.s: In spring, the Tatars and Bashkirs have a merry festival called Sabantuy. Its name means “festival of the plough”: when the fields are ploughed and sown, it is time to have fun. People run with an egg on a spoon, jump in sacks and climb a tall smooth pole. They also wrestle with belts. This wrestling is called kuresh. The winner is given a lovely embroidered towel, and sometimes even a live lamb.

ru-c-yolka-petr.s: A long time ago, more than three hundred years ago, Tsar Peter the Great decided to celebrate the New Year in winter, on the first of January. He ordered people to decorate houses and streets with branches of fir, pine and juniper. At first these were just green branches by the gates. Then people began to put a whole tree in the house and hang apples, nuts, candles and paper toys on it. That is how we got the New Year tree.

ru-c-kvas.s: Kvass is one of the oldest Russian drinks, and it is made from bread. You pour water over dry brown bread, add a starter, and the drink begins to bubble softly. In a day or two it turns sour-sweet and fizzy. People used to drink kvass on hot days in the hayfield and with their dinner. Kvass is also used for a cold summer soup called okroshka, with chopped cucumbers and spring onions in it.

ru-c-banya-venik.s: A Russian banya is a warm wooden hut full of hot steam. People steam themselves there with a broom made of birch or oak twigs, and its green leaves smell like a summer forest. The brooms are gathered in summer, tied in bunches and dried under the roof. Before the banya, the broom is soaked in boiling water, and a lovely smell fills the whole house. And when you have washed, people say kind words: “S legkim parom!”, which means “Enjoy your steam!”

ru-c-nalichniki.s: In Russian villages, people used to nail carved wooden frames around their windows. They are called nalichniki. The craftsmen carved suns, birds, flowers, mermaids and magical beasts on them. The wood came out as thin as lace, and the house looked smart, as if it were wearing a party dress. Nalichniki were painted in bright colours: blue, white and light blue. In the old days, people believed that the patterns kept the house safe, and everyone living in it.

ru-c-valenki.s: Valenki are made from sheep’s wool, and they have no seams at all. The master takes soft wool, wets it with hot water, and presses and rolls it with his hands for a long time. The wool sticks together by itself into thick, warm felt. The result is a boot that keeps out the cold even in hard frost. In the old days, valenki were often made exactly the same, so the right and the left were not different. They fitted themselves to the foot.

ru-c-pavlovo-platki.s: In the town of Pavlovsky Posad near Moscow, they make famous shawls. They are made of fine wool, and along the edge they have a long, fluffy fringe. The flowers on them are huge, like in a fairy-tale garden: roses, poppies, peonies. In the old days the pattern was printed on the cloth by hand, with wooden blocks. Such a shawl is warm and very pretty, and it is worn on the shoulders or on the head. Every shawl is like a bouquet that never wilts.

ru-c-palekh.s: In the village of Palekh, people paint on black lacquer boxes. The box is made of papier-mâché, which is pressed paper. It is covered with black lacquer, and the paints glow brightly on it, like precious stones. The masters mix their paints with egg yolk, and make their brushes from squirrel tails, so fine that you can paint every single eyelash. The heroes of Palekh pictures are fairy-tale knights, birds and troikas of horses. Often they use real gold for the patterns.

ru-c-zhostovo.s: In the village of Zhostovo near Moscow, people paint metal trays. The background is usually black, but it can also be green, red or blue. And on it is a huge bouquet: peonies, roses, tulips, berries. The master paints the flowers with wide brushstrokes straight from the brush, with no pencil drawing first. Then the trays are covered with lacquer, and they shine like a mirror. There are never two bouquets alike: every master has his own hand.

ru-c-vologda-kruzhevo.s: Vologda lace is made not with a needle but with little wooden sticks called bobbins. There can be several dozen of them! The lacemaker sits in front of a round cushion with the pattern pinned onto it. She quickly passes the bobbins from hand to hand, and they tap softly. The threads weave into a fine pattern: flowers, leaves, snowflakes. This lace is used to make collars, napkins and tablecloths. They say it looks like frost patterns on a window.

ru-c-gorodets.s: In the town of Gorodets on the Volga, people paint wooden boards, spinning-wheel seats and toys. The main heroes of the painting are a yellow horse, a rooster and huge flowers with round petals. The background is often yellow, like the sun, or light blue. The masters paint quickly, straight with the brush, and then outline the pattern with a black and a white line. The little horse comes out merry, as if it were dancing. In the old days, such painted boards hung on the walls of houses.

ru-c-bogorodsk.s: In the village of Bogorodskoye, people have carved funny toys from lime wood for a very long time. The most famous is “The Blacksmiths”: a little man and a bear stand on either side of an anvil. Under the toy there is a little bar with a ball. Pull it back and forth, and they hit with their hammers one after the other! Lime wood is soft and easy to carve, and the toy feels warm to the touch. In the old days, such toys were taken to fairs in sacks, and the village children were happy.

ru-c-troyka.s: A troika is three horses pulling together. The middle one trots steadily, and the two at the sides gallop, and all together they pull a sleigh or a carriage very fast. Over the middle horse hangs a tall wooden arch, and under it is a bell. It rings all along the road, and you can hear from far away that a troika is coming. The horses were decorated with ribbons, and in winter troikas with bells gave rides over the snow at festivals. The ringing carried through the whole village.

ru-c-tsar-kolokol.s: In Moscow, in the Kremlin, stands the biggest bell in the world: the Tsar Bell. It weighs about two hundred tonnes, like several dozen elephants, and is almost as tall as a two-storey house. But it has never rung. While it was still standing in the pit after being cast, there was a fire, and the bell cracked, and a huge piece broke off. Now the bell stands on a stone base, and you can look inside it as if it were a room. But in the Kremlin cathedrals other bells ring, and each one has its own voice.

ru-c-ilya-muromets.s: Byliny are old songs and tales about Russian heroes. They were not read, but sung to the gusli. The most famous hero is Ilya Muromets. He came from a village near the town of Murom, and, as the bylina says, for thirty years and three years he could not stand on his feet. Then wanderers gave him water to drink, and he became the strongest hero. He was kind and protected people. The old storytellers passed the byliny on by word of mouth.

ru-c-khomus.s: The Yakut people have an amazing musical instrument, the khomus. It is very small and fits in the palm of your hand. It is a metal frame with a thin little tongue in the middle. The musician presses the khomus to their teeth, plucks the tongue with a finger and changes the shape of their mouth. It sounds like something unusual: now the wind, now galloping horses, now birds chirping. The player’s mouth works like a little hall. In Yakutia there is even a museum of the khomus, and people of all ages play it.

ru-d-ciolkovsky.s: In the city of Kaluga lived a school teacher, Konstantin Tsiolkovsky. He taught children maths and physics, and in the evenings he dreamed up how people would fly to the stars. He was the first to suggest a rocket made of several parts: when one part burns up, it drops off, and the rocket becomes lighter. He also wrote: “The Earth is the cradle of mind, but you cannot live in a cradle for ever.” His house in Kaluga is still there, and people come to see it.

ru-d-sputnik.s: On 4 October 1957, Sergei Korolev’s rocket rose into the sky. It carried the world’s first artificial satellite of the Earth into orbit. It was a shiny metal ball the size of a big ball, with four long whiskers, which were aerials. It flew around the Earth and beeped: “beep-beep-beep”. Radio amateurs all over the world listened to these signals. And the word “sputnik” is now known in many languages.

ru-d-mendeleev.s: Dmitri Mendeleev invented a table in which all the chemical elements stand in order. That was in 1869. In the table he left empty boxes, for elements that people had not found yet! And he even said what they would be like. A few years later, scientists found gallium, scandium and germanium, and they turned out almost as he had written. And in his free time Mendeleev liked to make suitcases.

ru-d-lomonosov.s: Mikhail Lomonosov was born in a northern village by the sea, and became a great scientist. It was on his suggestion that a university was opened in Moscow, which now carries his name. In 1761 he watched through a telescope as the planet Venus passed across the disc of the Sun, and he noticed a thin glowing rim around it. Lomonosov understood: Venus has air, an atmosphere! He wrote about it, and the discovery was remembered.

ru-d-lobachevsky.s: Nikolai Lobachevsky worked almost all his life in Kazan, at the university, and for nineteen years he was the head there, the rector. He invented a new geometry. In ordinary geometry, two parallel lines never meet. But in his, parallel lines behaved differently, as on a curved surface. At first many people were surprised and did not believe him, but then this geometry helped scientists understand the world better. He is called the “Copernicus of geometry”.

ru-d-popov.s: The teacher and scientist Alexander Popov built a device that could hear far-off thunderstorms. Then he made Russia’s first radio from it. In 1896 he sent two words through the air, without wires: “Heinrich Hertz”, the name of the scientist who discovered radio waves. The signal travelled about two hundred and fifty metres, across the university yard. Since then, radio has sounded all over the world, and on 7 May Russia celebrates Radio Day.

ru-d-kulibin.s: The self-taught master Ivan Kulibin lived in Nizhny Novgorod and could make anything: clocks, bridges, even a carriage with pedals. His most famous marvel is a clock shaped like an egg, the size of a goose egg. He gave it to Empress Catherine. Every hour the clock played a tune, tiny doors opened, and little figures appeared. Today this clock is kept in St Petersburg, in the Hermitage.

ru-d-sikorsky.s: Igor Sikorsky dreamed of flying from childhood. In 1913 he built a huge aeroplane in Russia, the “Ilya Muromets”, with four engines! At that time many people did not believe that such a heavy aeroplane would get off the ground. And inside there was a real cabin: you could walk about in it, and the passengers sat in comfortable seats. Later Sikorsky went to America and built one of the first helicopters that could really be flown.

ru-d-balet.s: Ballerinas dance in special shoes, called pointe shoes, and stand on the very tips of their toes. A pair of pointe shoes does not last long: famous ballerinas sometimes need a new pair for every performance! In Russia there are famous theatres: the Bolshoi in Moscow and the Mariinsky in St Petersburg. In St Petersburg children learn to dance at the school named after Agrippina Vaganova. And “Swan Lake” and “The Nutcracker” are put on the Russian stage every winter.

ru-d-pushkin-licey.s: When little Sasha Pushkin was twelve, he went to study at the Lyceum in Tsarskoye Selo near St Petersburg. The Lyceum was a special school: the boys lived and studied there, and his friends grew up together with him. At fifteen, Pushkin read his poems at an exam, and the old famous poet Derzhavin listened. They say he was so delighted that he wanted to hug the boy. Today Tsarskoye Selo is part of the town of Pushkin.

ru-d-tolstoy.s: Leo Tolstoy lived on the estate of Yasnaya Polyana, where apple trees and birches grew. He opened a school there for village children and wrote books for them himself: an “ABC” and fairy tales like “The Three Bears”. And he loved to keep moving: he rode horses, walked many miles, and at 67 he learned to ride a bicycle! The house and garden of Yasnaya Polyana are open to visitors, and you can walk there.

ru-d-chekhov.s: Anton Chekhov was a doctor and a writer. For a time he lived on the Melikhovo estate, not far from Moscow. He planted trees, treated his neighbours and helped build schools for village children. And Chekhov had two dachshunds, with funny names: Brom and Quinine. These are two medicines, and Chekhov, as a doctor, liked to joke. The house in Melikhovo is now a museum, and visitors go there too.

ru-d-tretyakov.s: Pavel Tretyakov lived in Moscow and loved paintings very much. All his life he bought works by Russian artists, and they hung in his house. One day he decided to give the collection to everyone and handed it over to the city of Moscow. That is how the Tretyakov Gallery came about. In it you can see sad Alyonushka by the pond and the three heroes on horses. Every year millions of people come there, and children too.

ru-d-ledokol.s: An icebreaker is a ship that goes through ice. Its bow has a special shape: it rides up onto the ice and breaks it with its weight. In 1959, Russia built the world’s first nuclear icebreaker, the “Lenin”. It did not need to refuel often, like ordinary ships, so it could work for a long time far in the north. Icebreakers like this are based in Murmansk and help ships get through the Arctic Ocean.
a: It rides up with its bow and presses with its weight

ru-d-russky-most.s: In Vladivostok, a bridge was built to Russky Island. It holds a record: the span between its two towers is 1,104 metres, the longest span of any cable-stayed bridge in the world. The cables are thick steel ropes, which run from the tall towers to the road like rays. The towers are higher than three hundred metres. The bridge opened in 2012, and you can drive over the sea on it, with the waves sparkling all around.

ru-d-mir.s: “Mir” was the world’s first modular space station: it was put together in orbit, piece by piece, like a building set. Building began in 1986, and it worked for about fifteen years. The station flew over the Earth so fast that it went round in about an hour and a half, and the cosmonauts saw many sunrises and sunsets in a single day. Guests from different countries visited “Mir”. People were proud of it, and later the International Space Station was built from what had been learned.

sgp-a-merlion.s: By the water in Singapore stands an amazing statue. It has the head of a lion and the body of a fish, with scales and a tail. Its name is the Merlion. It is as tall as a three-storey house, and it spouts water from its mouth all day long. The fish reminds us that Singapore was once a fishing village. The lion reminds us that Singapore means “lion city”. There is also a tiny baby Merlion nearby, only two metres tall.
a: A fish body, with scales and a tail

sgp-a-supertrees.s: In the Gardens by the Bay stand the Supertrees, and they are not real trees. They are made of metal! They are between twenty-five and fifty metres tall. But real flowers and ferns climb up their trunks. Some of the tops have solar panels that collect sunlight in the daytime. In the evening the Supertrees glow in lots of colours, and a light show begins, with music. Everyone looks up and cannot look away.
a: They glow in lots of colours
They fold up their branches and go to sleep

sgp-a-jewel-changi.s: Changi Airport in Singapore has often been called one of the best airports in the world. It has a building called Jewel, and in the middle of it, inside a glass house, a huge waterfall tumbles down. It is called the Rain Vortex and it is about forty metres tall. The water pours from a hole in the roof, and a whole forest grows around it. In the evening, coloured lights shine on the waterfall. Your plane is not leaving for a long time, and you are already looking at a wonder!

sgp-b-hawker-centre.s: Singapore has hawker centres. These are huge shelters with lots of tables, and all around them are dozens of tiny kitchens. One family picks chicken rice, another a noodle soup, another little skewers, and everyone eats together at one table. In 2020 UNESCO added hawker culture to its list of the world’s special traditions, because people here share good food and eat together.
a: A shelter with tables and lots of tiny kitchens
A museum where you must not touch the food
A tower where they only make tea

sgp-b-durian.s: The durian is a big fruit covered in spikes, like a medieval club. Inside is soft yellow flesh, and many people think it tastes delicious. But the smell is so strong that it stays in a room for a long time. So in Singapore’s trains and in many hotels there are signs that say: no durians! People eat them outside, or at home where they can open a window.
a: The fruit has a very strong smell

sgp-c-night-safari.s: Singapore has a zoo that you visit after sunset. It is called the Night Safari. When it gets dark, the animals that slept all day wake up: tigers, hyenas, bats and flying squirrels. A little tram rides quietly along the path between the trees, and the lights are dim, like moonlight, so the animals are not scared. It is said to be the first zoo in the world that opens at night.
a: In the evening and at night

sgp-c-otters.s: In the bay in the middle of Singapore live smooth-coated otters. They stay in families: mum, dad and the pups. You can see them by the water. They dive for fish, warm up on the bank and call to each other with thin little voices. Their fur is short and smooth, and they have webbing between their toes, so they are very good swimmers. People stop to watch them, but you should not go close.

sgp-d-chinese-new-year.s: At the end of winter or the start of spring, Chinese New Year begins in Singapore. The streets are decorated with red lanterns, because red brings good luck. Children are given red envelopes with money inside. And in the squares, lions dance! Two dancers hide under a huge lion mask: one is the head and the other is the tail. To the beat of drums, the lion nods, jumps and “eats” green lettuce. That is for good luck too.

sgp-b-ice-cream-bread.s: On a street in Singapore, you might meet a seller with a big cool box. He takes out a slice of ice cream and puts it not in a wafer cone, but in a soft bun. Or he wraps it in bright bread: pink, yellow or green. Grown-ups and children both eat ice cream this way. On a hot day, a sweet bun with a cold filling is a real treat.

sgp-b-always-summer.s: Singapore sits almost in the middle of the Earth, near the equator. So there is no winter here. It is warm and damp all year, and rain can come in any month. It often starts after lunch. The sky goes dark, thunder rumbles and the rain drums on the roofs. People in Singapore do not mind. They hide under a shelter, and then the sun comes out again and the city sparkles.
a: It is almost on the equator, where it is always warm
A ship takes the winter away

sgp-a-mbs-ship.s: Look at the Marina Bay Sands hotel. Three tall towers stand side by side, and on top of them lies a long platform that looks like a ship. It is as if a huge ship sailed through the air and landed on three pillars! It is a whole park up high, with trees and paths. There is also a swimming pool with a view of the whole city. Only hotel guests can swim in it.

sgp-a-cloud-forest.s: In another glass dome of Gardens by the Bay lives the Cloud Forest. As soon as you step in, you see a mountain covered in green plants and orchids. And from the very top a waterfall tumbles down, right inside the building! It is about thirty-five metres high. A light mist floats around, like in the clouds, and it smells of damp leaves. You can go up the mountain in a lift and come down by a winding path.

sgp-b-four-languages.s: Singapore has four official languages: English, Chinese, Malay and Tamil. Most signs in the metro are in English, because almost everyone understands it. At school, children also learn the language of their family: some learn Chinese, others Malay, others Tamil. So a boy can chat with the lady next door in one language and with his granny at home in another.
a: The language of the people on the Moon

sgp-b-chilli-crab.s: Chilli crab is a festive dish in Singapore. A whole crab is cooked in a thick sauce of tomatoes, chilli and egg. The sauce is a little sweet, a little sour and not too spicy. You eat the crab with your hands, so there are napkins and crackers for the claws on the table. Soft buns are served with it: you dip them in the sauce and mop up every last drop.
a: You dip soft buns in it
You drink it through a bamboo straw
You spread it on a giant watermelon

sgp-b-mrt-driverless.s: Singapore has a metro called the MRT. Some of its lines run without a driver: a computer drives the train. If you stand by the very first door of the front carriage, you can look ahead through the glass, as if you were steering yourself. It is easy to pay with a travel card: you tap it on the reader at the entrance and the gate opens. You can pay on the bus with the same card.

sgp-c-jurong-birds.s: For many years Jurong Bird Park was home to birds in Singapore. Pink flamingos strolled about, and macaw parrots could repeat words. Flamingos are pink because of their food: shrimps and algae contain a colouring that tints the feathers. Flamingo chicks are grey! In 2023 Jurong closed, and the birds moved to a new park called Bird Paradise. It is in another part of the island.
a: Because of their food: shrimps and algae
They are born pink from the sun

sgp-c-penguins-sgp.s: Singapore is almost on the equator, and it is hot all year round. But penguins live in Bird Paradise! A cold house with icy water was built for them, just like the South Pole. Through the glass you can watch the penguins fly under the water like little torpedoes. There is even a dome where they swim right over the visitors’ heads. On land, penguins waddle funnily from foot to foot.
a: In a cool house with a glass wall
On the roof of a skyscraper

sgp-d-diwali.s: Diwali is an Indian festival of light. In Singapore, before it begins, the whole of Little India lights up: glowing arches and lanterns hang over the street. At home, people light small clay lamps. And by the front door they make a pattern from coloured powder or rice. It is called rangoli. People believe that kind light chases away the dark, and a pretty doorstep welcomes good luck.

sgp-b-kaya-toast.s: For breakfast, people in Singapore love kaya toast. Kaya is a soft jam made from coconut milk, eggs and sugar. Often the juice of green pandan leaves is added, and the jam turns a little green and smells lovely. Thin crunchy bread is spread with kaya and topped with a slice of cold butter. Soft-boiled eggs come with it: you pour them into a little saucer and dip the toast in.

sgp-c-sentosa-cable.s: Sentosa is an island next to Singapore. In Malay, its name means “peace and quiet”. You can get there by cable car: the cabins glide high above the harbour, ships sparkle below, and skyscrapers shine far away. Sentosa has sandy beaches with palm trees, where you can build sandcastles. The trip through the air is like a little adventure.

sp-sputnik.s: On 4 October 1957, a rocket rose into the sky and carried the world’s first satellite above the clouds. It was quite small: a shiny ball with four long antennas like whiskers. The satellite flew around the Earth and sent a signal: “beep-beep-beep”. People in many countries switched on their radios and listened to the sound of space. The satellite went around the Earth in about an hour and a half. The space age had begun.

sp-belka-strelka.s: On 19 August 1960, two dogs flew into space: Belka and Strelka. With them were mice, insects and even plants. The spaceship went around the Earth 17 times, then landed gently, and everyone came home safe and well. Belka and Strelka became famous all over the world. Later Strelka had puppies. One of them, called Pushinka, was given as a present to the family of the American President Kennedy, and lived in their home.

sp-gagarin.s: On 12 April 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space. He was born in a village, and as a boy he dreamed of aeroplanes. His spaceship was called Vostok. Before the launch, Gagarin said cheerfully: “Poyekhali!”, which means “Let’s go!” He flew once around the Earth, and the whole flight lasted 108 minutes. From space he saw our planet and said it was blue. Then he came safely back to Earth.

sp-armstrong.s: On 20 July 1969, the American spacecraft Apollo 11 landed on the Moon. Neil Armstrong climbed down the ladder and said: “That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.” So he became the first person on the Moon. Buzz Aldrin walked in the moon dust with him. They collected rocks and set up instruments. There is no wind and no rain on the Moon, so footprints do not get wiped away. They can stay for a very long time.
a: There is no wind or rain there

sp-eda.s: Long ago, astronauts ate from tubes, like toothpaste, but tasty: soup, mash and even juice. Today they also have ordinary meals in packets. Astronauts rarely take bread, because it makes crumbs. In weightlessness, crumbs do not fall down. They float in the air and could get into eyes or machines. So astronauts eat carefully and close their packets.

sp-mks.s: The International Space Station is a huge home that flies above the Earth. Astronauts from different countries live there, taking turns. The station goes around the Earth in about an hour and a half, so in one day they see about sixteen sunrises. If the sky is clear, you can even see the station from Earth. It is a bright dot that moves quickly across the sky and does not blink. Wave to it when you see it!

sp-sun-star.s: The Sun is a star, just like the stars you see at night. It is simply the closest one to us, so it shines so brightly and keeps us warm. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth. The Sun is huge: more than a million planets like ours would fit inside it. It is a ball of very hot gas. In the daytime the bright Sun hides the other stars, and we only see the blue sky.
a: It is the closest one to us
It is the biggest star in the world

sp-mars-rovers.s: On Mars, robots on wheels are at work: Mars rovers. Curiosity landed on Mars in 2012, and Perseverance in 2021. They have cameras, arms and tools to study red rocks and dust. Perseverance also brought a little helicopter called Ingenuity. It was the first helicopter to rise into the air over another planet. It flew very low, but it was a real flight!

sp-aurora.s: In the cold far north, for example in Norway or Iceland, green and pink ribbons of light sometimes spread across the sky. They move like huge curtains. These are the northern lights. The Sun sends tiny particles towards the Earth, and high above us they bump into the air, and the air starts to glow. The lights are most often green. The best time to see them is in winter, on a dark, frosty night.

sp-meteors.s: Sometimes at night a bright streak zooms across the sky. People call it a shooting star, but it is not a star. It is a meteor: a tiny grain of dust from space flies into the Earth’s air and flashes brightly high above us. It burns up before it reaches the ground. There are especially many in August, and this shower of stars is called the Perseids. There is a kind old saying: make a wish before the streak fades!
a: A tiny grain of dust that flashed in the air

sp-skafandr.s: A spacesuit is a space outfit, like a tiny spaceship you can climb into. In space there is no air, and the temperature changes a lot. So the suit has air to breathe, and the helmet has special glass that protects the eyes from the bright Sun. Under the suit, the astronaut wears special underwear with thin tubes, and cool water flows through them. The gloves are thick, but you can still hold tools in them.

sp-nevesomost.s: When you float, there is no “up” or “down”, so astronauts sleep in sleeping bags tied to the wall. Sometimes a sleeper’s arms float in front of them. Astronauts wash in a special way, too: water in space does not run down, it gathers into little balls. So they use wet towels and damp wipes. After brushing their teeth, they can wipe the toothpaste away carefully with a wipe.
a: In sleeping bags by the wall
On the ceiling with no bag

sp-galilei.s: A long time ago, in 1609, the scientist Galileo Galilei made a telescope and looked at the sky at night. He saw mountains on the Moon! And next to Jupiter he saw four little stars. They turned out to be moons of Jupiter. Every night they stood a bit differently, which meant they were going round the planet. Galileo drew it all in his notebook and showed people. That is how looking at the sky through a telescope began.

sp-hubble.s: The Hubble telescope flies around the Earth, high above the clouds and the air. From there the stars look very sharp, because air does not get in the way. It was launched in 1990 and is named after the scientist Edwin Hubble. The telescope has taken thousands of pictures: far-away planets, clouds of dust and huge islands of stars. Hubble’s photos look like bright paintings. Many of them hang in museums and appear in books.
a: Around the Earth, high above the air

sp-halley.s: A comet is a big ball of ice and dust. When it flies close to the Sun, the ice warms up and a bright tail appears around it. The tail always points away from the Sun, like a light puff of smoke in the wind. The most famous comet is named after a scientist called Halley. It comes back to Earth about every seventy-six years. It was last seen in 1986, and it will be seen next in 2061.

sp-star-colors.s: If you look closely, stars come in different colours. Some are white, others bluish, others yellow or orange, and some are reddish. The colour tells you how hot a star is. Blue stars are the hottest, yellow ones, like our Sun, are a bit less hot, and red stars are the coolest. It is like a campfire: the hottest flame is bluish, and glowing embers are red. Try to find a reddish star in the sky!

sp-constellations.s: A long time ago, people joined stars with pretend lines, and pictures appeared. They are called constellations. There is the Lion, the Swan, the Scorpion and the Great Bear. In the Great Bear, seven bright stars make a big ladle with a handle, also called the Plough. It is easy to find in the northern sky. The stars in a constellation are really far away from each other. From Earth they just look close together.

sp-milky-way.s: Far from the city lights, on a dark night, you can see a pale stripe in the sky, as if someone spilled milk. This is the Milky Way. It is really a huge number of stars, so far away that they blur into a misty path. Our Sun and the whole Earth live in this big family of stars, which is called a galaxy. It has hundreds of billions of stars. Seen from above, the galaxy looks like a pinwheel with curly arms.
a: Our galaxy, a huge group of stars

sp-voyagers.s: Two spacecraft called Voyager set off in 1977 and are still flying. They are farther from Earth than anything else: more than twenty billion kilometres! Each one carries a golden record with recordings. On it are greetings in many languages, the sound of rain and waves, birdsong and music. It is like a message in a bottle thrown into space: maybe someone will find it one day and listen.
a: Greetings, sounds of nature and music

sp-eclipse.s: Sometimes the Moon floats in front of the Sun and covers it. This is a solar eclipse. In the daytime it suddenly gets dim, like evening, and the birds go quiet. The Moon is much smaller than the Sun, but it is also much closer to us, so it can cover the Sun completely. But remember the most important rule: never look at the Sun without protection, not even during an eclipse. You need special dark glasses, and grown-ups give them out.
